doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Greenfield Village job with Mike Karoub's six-piece band
summary: As a young teenager he and Karoub won a summer job playing Dixieland at Greenfield Village, learning tunes fast and meeting older Detroit players.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: under interesting circumstances, because starting out as young as I did, my first big job — major, steady gig — was playing at a place called Greenfield Village in Dearborn, Michigan, which is where the Henry Ford Museum is. And my friend Mike Karoub, who I mentioned before, he always had a lot of chutzpah you know. And aside from being a great player, he was very ambitious, that may be a better word for it. But he decided, we had started playing around at PTA meetings, playing Dixieland arrangements that his father would help us dig up, and swing band stuff, big band stuff. We actually had a big band when I was in fifth grade and he was in sixth grade, playing big band classics. And we decided it was easier to have like a six piece group because there were six people who could improvise. You know the rest were sort of like scuffling along you know.
No one’s mother would let them come to rehearsal.

It was hard. A big band is always a hard thing to schedule and keep together. It’s a lot of logistics involved. Six people is a little less complicated and we could also, we just were gravitating toward that kind of music anyway. So he decided he’d call up Greenfield Village, because it was kind of like this sort of trip back into time sort of place. And I said, “Well what you need there is a Dixieland band, you know, to play outside and down by the river there.” They had a gazebo, and they said, “That’s an interesting idea, so why don’t you come in and audition.” So we went in and auditioned and played like the six songs that we knew, or whatever it was at that point. And it went well and they hired us and they said, “Great, you’re going to be playing six days a week, five hours a day, for the summer.”

I was, I’m trying to remember. I was either going into seventh grade — no, going into eighth grade I think, yeah. Somewhere between seventh and eighth grade. And so all of a sudden, here we are playing five hours a day, six days a week, and we got pretty tired of those — well it might have been a dozen songs or something that we knew by heart and then we had some arrangements. So we just started finding ways, whatever we could, to buy arrangements of old tunes that we liked, and also just learn things from records and lead sheets and sheet music, and we just sort of helped each other through it and learned a lot of songs in a hurry, mostly just to keep ourselves from going crazy and playing the same songs all the time.
Did you get any press from that? I would imagine that, you know, this young group of kids in there.

Yeah. We also started to get to know more of the musicians around town because even then we’d have to sub out some dates, because whenever so-and-so would have a football game or a baseball game or whatever, a family commitment or something like that. So we started to get to know some of the better, older players around town, because there wasn’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

anything in our contract that it had to be kids playing. So I mean they liked that, I think it was one of the selling points. But anyway, so we got to know a lot of the players around Detroit and there was quite a few, and there still are quite a few good players of all different styles there. It’s always been a good music city.
